article.headline: The Book of Color — An Interactive Essay on Color Theory
article.description: Where color comes from, how the eye builds it, and the quiet geometry that makes some colors sing together.

hero.lede: Color is not a property of things. It is an event — a meeting of light, matter, and mind. This is a field guide to that event.
hero.greynoteBody: Every surface here — every panel, button, and frame — is deliberately grey. A colored interface would quietly distort your judgment of the colors it surrounds. The only saturated thing on this page is the color we are discussing.

ch1.title: Light
ch1.standfirst: There is no red in a rose.
ch1.leadIn: A rose contains no color. What it has is a surface that absorbs most of the light striking it and throws back the rest — chiefly the long waves we have learned to call red. The color is not in the flower. It is not even in the light. It is in the meeting.
ch1.newton: In 1666 Isaac Newton darkened a room, let a single beam of sunlight through a prism, and watched it fan into an ordered band of color. The prism, he argued in Opticks (1704), adds nothing. White light is already a crowd of colors travelling together; the glass merely bends each by a different amount and so pulls the crowd apart.
ch1.wavelengthIntro: Each pure color in that band corresponds to a single wavelength of light — a spectral color. The eye answers to a narrow ribbon of wavelengths, roughly 380 nanometres (violet) to 700 (red), a sliver of the electromagnetic spectrum, which runs from radio waves kilometres long to gamma rays smaller than an atom. Drag across that ribbon below.
ch1.abney: Newton showed the line, but the eye is not literal about it. Take a single pure wavelength — a narrow band of blue at 475 nm, say — and dilute it with a little white light. By the physics, you are just adding broad-spectrum white to a narrow blue, and the wavelength of the peak does not move. But the perceived hue moves. The blue, mixed with white, drifts subtly toward violet; a pure yellow drifts toward orange. The effect was named for the nineteenth-century British physicist William de Wiveleslie Abney, who measured it in 1909. It is one of several reminders that the diagram in our heads is not the diagram on the spectroscope.
ch1.planck: One more correction before the wheel. Pure wavelengths are rare in nature; almost every light we ever see is a distribution across many wavelengths at once. The most common natural distribution is the glow of a hot body. Heat any black surface — a filament, a candle wick, the surface of a star — and as the temperature rises, the radiation it gives off shifts from invisible infrared up through dull red, glowing orange, white, and at very high temperatures into the blue. The exact spectrum at each temperature is given by Planck's law (1900), and the curve every temperature traces in chromaticity coordinates is called the Planckian locus. It is the spine of color temperature.

prism.title: Newton's Prism
prism.hint: Drag the slider · open or close the apex
prism.svgAria: A glass prism with horizontal white light entering its left face and a rainbow fan exiting the right. As the apex-angle slider widens, the fan opens further; as it narrows, the fan tightens.

prism.cap: White light is not white the way water is wet — it is a coexistence of every visible wavelength. Glass bends each wavelength by a slightly different amount, and the small bend at each face compounds into a visible fan. Newton called what came out the other side a spectrum; the rainbow on a wall is the same demonstration written by the sky.

abney.title: The Abney effect
abney.hint: Dilute a pure wavelength with white · watch the hue drift
abney.stageAria: Two coloured patches side by side. The left patch shows a pure wavelength diluted with white light, with the colour drifting subtly toward a different hue as more white is added (the Abney effect). The right patch shows the same wavelength with the perceived hue corrected back to the pure colour. Slide between zero and one hundred percent white admixture.
abney.ariaWhite: Percent white light added to the pure wavelength
abney.cap: A pure spectral wavelength, diluted with increasing amounts of white light. The left patch is the physically correct mixture — at high white admixture the perceived hue drifts toward an adjacent region of the wheel (blue toward violet, yellow toward orange). The right patch holds the perceived hue constant by walking back along the Abney correction. The lines on CIE 1931 that connect equal-perceived-hue points are called lines of constant hue; they are noticeably curved, not the straight radii one might expect.

planck.title: The Planckian locus
planck.hint: Slide the temperature · watch the glow shift
planck.stageAria: A simulation of black-body radiation. On the left, a glowing square shows the colour of a black body at the selected temperature, from dull red below 2000 K through orange, white near 6500 K, and into pale blue above 10,000 K. On the right, a small wavelength-versus-intensity graph shows the Planck spectrum at the same temperature, with the peak shifting from infrared into the visible and then into the violet end as temperature rises.
planck.cap: A candle flame is about 1850 K (warm orange); a tungsten bulb 2700–3000 K; midday sunlight at the equator is near 5500–6000 K; the standard daylight reference D65 is 6504 K; the dim blue of a clear north sky can exceed 15,000 K. Note how the painter's intuition (red = warm, blue = cool) inverts the physics (red = cool body, blue = hot body); the painter speaks of skin and fire, the physicist speaks of stars and filaments.

note.label: Hold this thought
note.body: The spectrum is a line. It has two ends — deep violet and deep red — and they sit at its opposite ends. Yet every color wheel you have ever seen joins them into a loop. Who authorized that? Chapter Four answers. Chapter Two supplies the motive.

ch2.title: The Eye
ch2.leadIn: The retina does not measure wavelength. It cannot. At the back of the eye sit three kinds of cone cells, and each is simply a bucket that fills with light — one tuned to short wavelengths (S), one to medium (M), one to long (L). Light of one wavelength arrives; the three buckets fill to three different levels; and those three numbers are the entire message sent to the brain.
ch2.trichromatic: From three numbers, the brain manufactures every color you have ever seen. This is the heart of trichromatic vision, first proposed by Thomas Young, refined by Helmholtz, confirmed a century later under the microscope. Set the wavelength below and watch the three cones respond.
ch2.metamerismIntro: Two far-reaching consequences follow from a three-number eye.
ch2.metamerismBody: The first is metamerism. If two completely different mixtures of light happen to fill the three buckets to the same three levels, they are — to you — the same color. Not similar. Identical. The eye has no deeper truth to consult.
ch2.spectralIntro: The two lights above are a single trick told with beams. The same trick happens with surfaces. Two pigments built from completely different spectra can agree perfectly under one light — and split apart the moment the light changes. Industry calls this the working form of metamerism, and it is the reason a fabric matched under the store's fluorescents looks wrong by the window at home.
ch2.magenta: The second consequence is stranger still: magenta. Look for it on the spectrum in Chapter One — you will not find it. There is no wavelength of magenta. It is the color the brain produces when the long and short cones are both excited while the medium cone is left far behind — that is, when the eye receives the two ends of the spectrum at once, with little from its middle. Magenta is extra-spectral — a color with no wavelength of its own, stitched by the brain from the spectrum's two ends.
ch2.adaptation: And the brain does more than invent: it also balances. Step out of an incandescent room into the daylight and for an instant everything seems too blue; a minute later it is back to itself. The eye rebalances the light by which it sees, so a sheet of paper stays white under any sun. The mechanism is called chromatic adaptation, and it runs, quietly, every moment of waking life.
ch2.adaptationRebound: Try this with the slider above: settle on one extreme — say 9000 K, a cool sky — and stare at the framed grey for thirty seconds, then swing it sharply to 2500 K, a warm candle. For a few moments every patch will look exaggeratedly warm — the grey will glow faintly pink, the reds will deepen — and then your eye will catch up and the room will normalise. That brief, hot moment is the rebound: the visual system, locked onto the cool reference, takes a second to release its compensation when the reference jumps. Chromatic adaptation is not a switch but a slow loop.
ch2.rods: In the other direction, when the light fades, the eye is built to fail gracefully. The cones — the daylight cells of the previous figure — need light to fire, and at dusk they begin to hand off to a second crew: the rods, more numerous, far more sensitive, and blind to colour. The handoff shifts what is bright. Cones peak in sensitivity at the long wavelengths; rods peak near 498 nanometres, well down the spectrum. So in the day a red poppy glows; at dusk it darkens first, while the greens and blues of the leaves and sky beside it hold on into the last light. The Czech anatomist Jan Evangelista Purkinje noticed the effect on his walks in 1819, and the shift has carried his name ever since.
ch2.closing: And that is the motive we were promised. Because the two ends of the spectral line, violet and red, can be seen together as a single new color, the line is free to curl around and close. The next chapters bend it into a wheel — and then open the wheel into a space.
ch2.benham: A century before Purkinje, in 1894, the English toy-maker Charles Benham noticed something stranger. A disk painted in only black and white — half of it solid black, the other half scored with a few thin black arcs at different radii — spun at the right speed appears to flash colour. Pale yellow at the outermost arcs, dim red toward the centre, blue if you reverse the spin. The colours are Fechner colours, named for the nineteenth-century psychophysicist Gustav Fechner, who described them in 1838. They are produced not by the disk but by the eye: the cones respond at slightly different speeds, so a black arc sweeping the retina pulses the channels out of phase, and the brain reads the unmatched signal as a pigment that is not there. The disk below is a reduced version of Benham's original — change the spin and watch a still grey ring colour itself.
ch2.bezoldBrucke: Light level changes lightness, as Purkinje saw. It also subtly changes hue. Take a single pure wavelength and crank up the brightness, and the colour does not stay put: a yellowish-green drifts toward pure yellow, a violet drifts toward blue, an orange drifts toward yellow. The effect was measured by the German physicists Wilhelm von Bezold and Ernst Brücke in 1873 and has carried both their names ever since. Three special wavelengths — near 478 nm, 503 nm, and 578 nm — sit on it and do not move; these invariant points are the boundaries of the opponent channels we will meet at the end of Chapter Eight. Push the slider and you can measure the drift yourself.

adapt.hint: Drag the slider · light from warm to cool
adapt.sceneAria: A row of seven coloured patches under one illuminant. As the colour-temperature slider moves, every patch shifts together; the framed centre patch is a fixed neutral grey that would, in real life, still look grey to a fully adapted observer.
adapt.cap: Each square is a fixed pigment; only the light changes. In a real room your brain would almost entirely undo this shift — the framed grey would stay grey. The page has no brain to do it for you, so watch the grey wander as the light warms or cools.

purkinje.title: The Purkinje Shift
purkinje.hint: Drag the slider · noon toward midnight
purkinje.sceneAria: A row of six coloured patches — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. As the light-level slider falls from day to night, the patches dim unequally: the warm end (red and orange) darkens first and fastest, while the cool end (greens and blues) dims more slowly and is the last to fade.
purkinje.ambientLabel: Ambient light, from full day to deep night
purkinje.cap: The same six pigments at every light level. As the rods take over, the warm end of the spectrum — reds and oranges — sinks first into the dark, while the cool end — greens and blues — lingers longest. The phenomenon is why some modern emergency fleets have moved to a Purkinje-friendly fluorescent yellow-green for high-visibility work, even where red remains the tradition.

benham.title: Benham's top
benham.hint: Spin the disk · see colour from nothing
benham.stageAria: A black-and-white disk modelled on Charles Benham's 1894 top: half the disk is solid black, the other half is scored with thin black arcs at three different radii. When the disk is spun, the eye sees pale colour at the moving arcs — yellow at the outer ring, red in the middle, blue near the centre — even though no ink on the disk is coloured. Slowing or reversing the spin changes which colour appears at each ring.
benham.speedRangeAria: Spin speed in rotations per minute, 0 (stopped) to 300
benham.cap: Charles Benham's 1894 artificial spectrum top — a disk painted only in black and white that, when spun, produces apparent colour at the moving arcs. The colour comes from the eye, not the disk: the L, M, and S cones differ slightly in response time, so a sweeping black-and-white edge pulses them out of phase. The brain integrates the mismatched timing as a hue — pale yellow at the outer arcs, dim red middle, blue near the centre. The effect is called Fechner colour, after Gustav Fechner, who described it in 1838. On most modern screens the colour is fainter than on the original spinning paper disk, because LCD refresh and pixel response interfere with the cone-timing trick; a high-refresh OLED shows it best.

bezoldBrucke.title: The Bezold–Brücke shift
bezoldBrucke.hint: Boost the luminance · the perceived hue drifts
bezoldBrucke.stageAria: Two coloured patches side by side, both starting at the same chosen wavelength. The left patch shows the colour at a low reference luminance; the right patch shows the same wavelength at a higher luminance. As the luminance slider is pushed up, the right patch drifts in hue: reds toward yellow, greens toward yellow, violets toward blue. At three special wavelengths (near 478, 503, and 578 nanometres) the patches stay identical no matter the luminance.
bezoldBrucke.cap: A single pure wavelength shown at two luminances. The left patch is the reference; the right patch is the same wavelength played louder. Below about 500 nm the brightened patch drifts toward blue; above about 580 nm it drifts toward yellow. Try 478 nm, 503 nm, or 578 nm — the three invariant points on the Bezold–Brücke curve — and the two patches stay in lockstep no matter how loud the second one gets. The invariants mark where the L–M and S–(L+M) opponent channels see zero imbalance; everywhere else the system reads a tilt and reports it as hue.

ch3.title: Mixing
ch3.standfirst: Two opposite logics — and a paintbox that disagrees with a screen.
ch3.leadIn: Ask a child what red and green make. Brown, they say, and they are right — they have a paintbox. Ask a lighting engineer: yellow, they say, and they are also right — they have a stage. Both answers are correct because there are two entirely opposite ways to make a color, and they run in opposite directions.
ch3.additiveBody: Additive mixing is the logic of light. Begin in darkness and add. Each beam you add can only make things brighter. Red light and green light overlap into yellow; add blue and you arrive at white. This is the logic of screens, projectors, and stage lights — and of sunlight, a broad blend of wavelengths spanning the whole visible range. Drag the three lights together below.
ch3.subtractiveBody: Subtractive mixing is the logic of pigment. Begin with white paper — light already complete — and take away. Every pigment is a filter: it absorbs, subtracts, part of the spectrum and reflects the remainder. Lay cyan over yellow and between them they remove the red and the blue, leaving green. Pile all three and almost nothing escapes: you approach black. This is the logic of printing inks and transparent filters — exact for layered cyan, magenta, and yellow, and a fair first model for paint as well.
ch3.paintBody: But paint, in truth, is stranger. Light does not pass through it like a filter; it enters the wet film, bounces off countless pigment grains, and only some of it returns. The cyan and yellow of a printer's ink are engineered so the filter model holds — between them they let only green through. Mix the painter's ultramarine blue and cadmium yellow and the eye still sees green; multiply those same two as numbers on a screen and they fall into a near-black mud. Paul Kubelka and Franz Munk wrote down the older arithmetic in 1931 — the same year the chromaticity diagram of Chapter Seven was drawn — and it remains the working model of every painter's palette to this day.
ch3.maxwellIntro: Light and pigment are the two arithmetics taught above. There is a third, born of motion. James Clerk Maxwell, in the early 1860s, mounted painted sectors on a spinning top and discovered that the eye sums them in time: a disc split between red and green, spun fast enough, settles into yellow — not on the disc but in the retina, which cannot keep up with the alternation. This is temporal additive mixing: the eye, asked to integrate too quickly, surrenders and averages.
ch3.closing: The primaries differ because the logics differ. Light builds from red, green, blue; printing ink from cyan, magenta, yellow; the painter's tubes from a red, a yellow, and a blue. Neither set is sacred — there is no such thing as the primary colors, only the right primaries for the direction you are travelling. Which raises the question the next chapter is built on: if the primaries are a choice, what shape should we arrange them in?

The patch on the right shows what your visual cortex would resolve at an infinite refresh rate.

ch4.title: The Wheel
ch4.standfirst: Bend the line until its two ends touch.
ch4.leadIn: A spectrum is a line, and a line has ends. Chapter One left us with that discomfort: deep violet at one extreme, deep red at the other, and no road between them. Chapter Two supplied the bridge — magenta, the extra-spectral color the eye builds when only the spectrum's two ends are lit. Magenta is the splice. With it, the line can be lifted at both ends and curved until red meets violet, and the spectrum closes into a ring with no beginning and no end.
ch4.circleBody: That ring is the color wheel — not a discovery but an invention, and a useful one. On a wheel every hue has neighbours to either side and exactly one color facing it across the centre: its complement. Turn the marker below, and switch the wheel between its two great traditions.
ch4.primariesBody: Where to place the hues, and which to crown as primary, has never been settled — because it cannot be. It is a choice, and history has made it more than once.
ch4.newtonGoetheItten: In 1704 Isaac Newton drew the first color circle, in his Opticks, and — being Newton — could not resist a deeper claim: he gave his seven colors arcs sized to the seven steps of a musical scale, so that the spectrum and the octave might share one geometry. (The companion to this essay, The Circle of Fifths, walks the musician's version of that same circle.) A century on, Goethe — who distrusted Newton — built a smaller wheel of six and paired every color with a feeling. And at the Bauhaus, Johannes Itten taught with a wheel of twelve, raised on the painter's primaries: red, yellow, blue.
ch4.physicistPainter: Those are not the physicist's primaries. Light mixes from red, green, and blue; pigment, as Chapter Three showed, from cyan, magenta, and yellow; the studio tradition keeps red, yellow, and blue. Switch the wheel above between the light arrangement and the painter's, and watch a color's complement change under your eye — red faces cyan on the one wheel and green on the other. Neither is an error. They are answers to different questions.

note.label: Toward a space
note.body: A wheel holds every hue — but only hue. It has nothing to say about a pale rose beside a deep crimson, or a dull brick beside a vivid scarlet: on the wheel, all of them are simply red. To hold those differences the wheel must grow two further dimensions. Chapter Five gives it depth.

ch5.title: Three Dimensions
ch5.standfirst: Hue is one number. A color needs three.
ch5.leadIn: The wheel of Chapter Four is a magnificent simplification, and like every simplification it lies a little. It shows each hue, and only hue. But say a color aloud — red — and you have named almost nothing. A fire engine, a clay roof tile, the pink lining of a shell, a dried bloodstain: every one of them is red, and no two are the same color.
ch5.valueChroma: What separates them are two further measurements. The first is value — how light or dark the color is, its place on the road from black to white. The second is chroma — how pure or how muted it is, its distance from a neutral grey. Hue, value, chroma: three numbers, three independent directions. Color is not a wheel. It is a solid — the wheel was a slice through it, taken at one value.
ch5.munsellBody: The first to map this solid by measurement rather than by geometry was Albert Munsell, a painter and teacher, around 1905. He had lost patience with color names that meant nothing dependable — "rose", "straw", "drab" — and gave each color three plain coordinates instead: hue, value, chroma. His own model was not a tidy sphere or cylinder but a lopsided tree, and honestly so — a vivid yellow is light and a vivid blue is dark, so the hues swell outward at different heights. The space of color has a real and irregular shape, and Munsell drew it as it is.
ch5.tintShadeTone: Within that solid, painters have always known three ways to move a color. A tint adds white and lifts it toward the light. A shade adds black and lowers it toward the dark. A tone adds grey and draws it inward, toward the colorless core. Choose a color in the panel below — its hue, then how saturated and how light it is — and watch the three paths open from it.

The two are the same set of colours, fit to two different rulers. Drag either canvas to rotate them together; pull the slider to lift the top and see inside. The asymmetry on the right is Munsell's tree, drawn by mathematics this time.

note.label: From one color to many
note.body: We can now fix any single color exactly — one point, three coordinates, somewhere in the solid. But a color is rarely chosen alone. Almost always it is chosen for company, to be set beside others. Chapter Six asks which colors belong together, and why.

ch6.title: Harmony
ch6.standfirst: Colors keep their best company by geometry.
ch6.leadIn: A color is almost never met alone. A poster, a room, a painting, a page like this one — each is a chord of several colors sounded together, and some chords ring while others jar. For most of history, knowing which was which was called taste, and could not be taught. The color wheel changed that: it turned the question into geometry. Harmonious colors, it proposed, are simply the ones that stand in a clean, repeatable figure on the wheel.
ch6.chooseBody: Choose a base color and a figure below. The wheel draws the shape; the palette and the small composition beside it show those colors at work.
ch6.temperamentBody: Each figure has a temperament. Complementary colors sit straight across from each other — as far apart in hue as two colors can be — and so meet the eye with the sharpest contrast a pair can hold; set side by side they seem to buzz along their border, a tension Chapter Eight will explain. Analogous colors are neighbours, of one family, and lie quietly together. Triadic and the four-cornered figures spread the circle evenly: vivid, yet balanced, because no direction is favoured. Split-complementary keeps a complement's tension but softens its bluntness. Monochromatic gives up hue contrast altogether and works in value and chroma alone — the most serene scheme of all.
ch6.grammarBody: None of this is a law. It is a grammar — the same kind of thing as the chord progressions in this essay's musical companion, The Circle of Fifths. A grammar does not write the sentence; it tells you which sentences will be understood. The finest color, like the finest writing, often comes from knowing the rule exactly — and then, for a reason, breaking it.
ch6.newton: The musical analogy is not incidental. Isaac Newton, in Opticks (1704), already divided his prism's spectrum into seven bands and proposed that each band corresponded to a step of the diatonic scale — red to do, orange to re, and so on up to violet at ti. The mapping is arbitrary in its specifics (Newton mostly wanted seven of something, and the seven notes were at hand), but the underlying intuition — that color shares the structure of a chord — has never gone away. Press a key below and you can hear what Newton heard.

harmony.title: The Harmony Explorer
harmony.hint: Drag the marker · or focus it and use ← →
harmony.capInitial: Three hues an equal third of the circle apart — balanced, lively, and stable.

newtonKeyboard.title: Newton's color-music keyboard
newtonKeyboard.hint: Click a key · hear a note, see its colour
newtonKeyboard.stageAria: A seven-key piano keyboard, one octave from C to B. Each key is bordered with the colour Newton assigned to it in 1704: C red, D orange, E yellow, F green, G blue, A indigo, B violet. Clicking a key plays a sine-wave tone at the corresponding musical pitch and lights the colour above. Pressing more than one key at a time blends the colours additively on the panel above.
newtonKeyboard.cap: Newton mapped the seven notes of the diatonic scale (C major, do–re–mi–fa–sol–la–ti) onto the seven bands he drew across his prism's spectrum, in Opticks (1704). Pressing more than one key sounds the chord and adds the colours on the panel above — the music of a C-major triad is the additive mix of red, yellow, and blue. Newton's pairing is historically influential and physically arbitrary; the frequencies of audible sound and visible light differ by a factor of more than ten trillion. But the structural intuition — that harmony is a matter of intervals, in colour as in tone — has outlived the arithmetic.

note.label: A crack in the wheel
note.body: Every figure drawn on that wheel was measured in equal degrees of hue — as though a step of thirty degrees were the same size everywhere on the circle. It is not. The wheel we have used is spaced evenly by number, not by the eye. Chapter Seven rebuilds the space to the eye's own measure.

ch7.title: Color Spaces
ch7.standfirst: A map is only as honest as its grid.
ch7.leadIn: Chapter Six ended on a confession: the wheel was spaced by number, not by the eye. So was the solid of Chapter Five. A color space is simply a coordinate system for color — a way to pin any color with a short list of numbers — and the only question worth asking of one is whether its numbers agree with what you see.
ch7.rgbHslBody: The most familiar is RGB: three values, nought to two hundred and fifty-five, one for each primary light. It is the native tongue of screens, and perfectly honest about the machine — but not about the eye. HSL — hue, saturation, lightness — was invented to be kinder to people, and it is more intuitive to handle. But its lightness is a polite fiction. Ask HSL for fifty percent lightness and it will hand you a brilliant yellow and a deep, dim blue with equal confidence, and call them equals.
ch7.hkIntro: HSL is at least honest about saying lightness. The deeper trick is that even within the eye's own perceptual lightness — even OKLCH's L — there is a residual nudge that chroma itself gives to perceived brightness. A vividly saturated colour, all else equal, looks lighter than its grey twin. Hermann von Helmholtz and Friedrich Kohlrausch noted the effect in 1907; the eye, it turns out, refuses to weigh colour as a single number.
ch7.cieIntro: Honest maps had been attempted before. In 1931 the Commission internationale de l'éclairage drew the first of them from real measurements of human vision — the chromaticity diagram below, a horseshoe that gathers every hue and every saturation a person can see into one shape, the whole of color laid flat.
ch7.gamutBody: Its curved rim is the pure light of Chapter One, the spectrum bent into an arc; its straight foot is the purples, which have no wavelength and live only in the mind. No screen and no ink can reproduce the whole of it; each reaches only its own patch — a triangle for the screens, a more irregular shape for the printer — and everything beyond that patch is a color you can see but cannot show. That shortfall is what the word gamut names. The diagram was a monument — and yet still uneven in its corners: equal distances across it did not mean equal differences to the eye. The repair took most of a century.
ch7.gamutIntro: The horseshoe above is abstract — every chromaticity a human can see, with the three gamuts marked. The viewfinder below is concrete: an image painted directly into the screen's wide-gamut Display P3 canvas, with deliberate flecks of colour outside sRGB. Drag the circular magnifier across it and watch the pixels it captures appear, in real time, as dots on the horseshoe. Switch the target gamut to see which dots fall outside — those are the colours your screen would crush, or the printer would invent a stand-in for, on the way to its surface.
ch7.oklabBody: In 2020 Björn Ottosson published OKLab, and its cylindrical form OKLCH — a space tuned so that equal steps look equal, and lightness, at last, means lightness. It has since been written into the CSS standard and runs in almost every browser made. It is the color wheel of Chapter Four and the solid of Chapter Five, built once more — and measured, this time, not by number but by the eye.
ch7.helmholtzKohlrausch: One last warning before we leave the spaces. Even OKLCH, which promises that equal numbers in L are equal in perceived lightness, has a small lie in it: highly saturated colours look brighter than their measured luminance predicts. The effect was first measured by Hermann von Helmholtz in the 1850s and refined by F. Kohlrausch in 1920, and is called the Helmholtz–Kohlrausch effect. Place a saturated red square and a neutral grey square side by side and adjust their luminances until they look equally bright. Then read the luminance meter: the red has substantially less physical light coming off it than the grey. The match is in the eye; the meter never agrees.

hslVsOk.title: HSL Against OKLCH
hslVsOk.hint: Drag the slider to read any hue
hslVsOk.canvasAria: Two strips, each sweeping through every hue. The HSL strip, held at lightness 50 percent, varies wildly in perceived brightness; the OKLCH strip, held at lightness 70 percent, stays perceptually even.
hslVsOk.hueLabel: Hue, the same step everywhere on the circle
hslVsOk.cap: Each pair of bands runs through every hue. The wide band is the color; the narrow band below it is the lightness your eye actually perceives. The HSL band heaves from bright to dark and back — its "50%" names a different brightness at every hue. The OKLCH band holds level: its lightness is the eye's. (The two are set at different numbers on purpose — HSL's "50%" has no fixed perceptual meaning, so matching the numbers would only compare brightnesses, not test the claim.)

hk.title: The Helmholtz–Kohlrausch Effect
hk.hint: Match the grey to the colour's brightness — by eye
hk.patchAriaGrey: Neutral grey patch — drag the grey lightness slider to set it
hk.patchAriaColor: Saturated colour patch, fixed at OKLCH L equals 0.60
hk.labelGreyL: Grey lightness — slide until the two patches feel equally bright
hk.ariaChroma: Chroma of the colour in OKLCH units
hk.ariaGreyL: OKLCH L of the neutral grey
hk.cap: Both swatches share one constraint: the colour is fixed at OKLCH L = 0.60. Your task is to slide the grey's lightness until the two feel equally bright to your eye, then press Reveal. The verdict shows how much extra lightness — in OKLCH and in raw luminance Y — you had to give the grey to match a colour the eye insists is brighter than its numbers say. The boost depends on hue (it is strongest in the deep blues and reds) and grows with chroma. Calibration disclaimer: the exact match depends on your monitor and ambient light; what matters is the direction and rough magnitude.

cie.title: The 1931 Horseshoe
cie.hint: Drag the slider along the spectrum
cie.canvasAria: The CIE 1931 chromaticity diagram. A horseshoe-shaped field holds every chromaticity the human eye can see; its curved rim is the pure spectral wavelengths from 380 to 700 nanometres, and the straight edge across its foot is the purples, which have no wavelength of their own. Inside the field, three triangles mark working gamuts: the solid triangle is standard sRGB, the dashed one is the wider Display P3, and the dotted one — smaller than either — is a C/M/Y approximation of the four-colour offset-print gamut, whose true shape is a six-vertex polygon. The whole region between the triangles and the rim is visible to the eye but lies beyond what a screen can show, and is drawn pale.
cie.nmLabel: A pure wavelength, marked on the rim
cie.cap: Drag the slider to walk the marker along the rim — each point one pure wavelength, the spectrum of Chapter One curled into an arc. The three triangles are working gamuts: solid is sRGB, the standard of the web; dashed is the wider Display P3 of recent screens; the smaller dotted triangle is a C/M/Y approximation of the offset-print gamut (its true shape is a six-vertex polygon — the triangle has roughly the right size, not the right shape). This is why a vivid screen graphic loses some life when it reaches a printed page. Every colour outside the solid sRGB triangle is drawn pale on purpose: it lies beyond the gamut this page is itself drawn in, so the diagram can only gesture toward a colour it cannot truly show.

gamutView.title: The Gamut Viewfinder
gamutView.hint: Drag the lens · switch the target gamut
gamutView.imgAria: A synthetic wide-gamut colour image painted directly into a Display P3 canvas. Some regions contain colours outside the sRGB triangle. Drag or focus to position the circular magnifier.
gamutView.cieAria: The CIE 1931 chromaticity diagram. Pixels currently under the magnifier appear as dots; pixels outside the chosen target gamut are highlighted with a red outline.
gamutView.targetAriaGroup: Target gamut for the warning outline
gamutView.cap: The source canvas is rendered in Display P3 where the browser supports it (Safari 15+, Chrome 110+, Firefox 113+); on older browsers it falls back to sRGB and the out-of-gamut warnings stay quiet. Each dot on the horseshoe is one pixel under the magnifier, transformed through the standard sRGB (or P3) matrix into CIE XYZ and then into xy. The three triangles are the same as in the horseshoe above. The red outline counts how many of the pixels you have caught lie outside whichever target you choose — vivid greens and cyans usually surrender to sRGB first; deep oranges and reds tend to die in the move to CMYK.

helmholtzKohlrausch.title: The Helmholtz–Kohlrausch effect
helmholtzKohlrausch.hint: Match the brightness · then read the luminance gap
helmholtzKohlrausch.stageAria: A saturated coloured square on the left next to a neutral grey square on the right. Two sliders set the colour's hue and the grey's luminance independently. The reader's task is to drag the grey luminance until the two squares look equally bright; the readout reports the physical luminance of each square. For high-chroma colours the matching grey is consistently darker — sometimes by 20 to 40 percent — than the coloured square, even though the brain reads them as equally bright. That gap is the Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect.
helmholtzKohlrausch.labelL: Grey lightness (match the brightness by eye)
helmholtzKohlrausch.ariaHue: Hue of the coloured patch in degrees, 0 to 360
helmholtzKohlrausch.cap: If the match is genuine, the gap reads positive — the saturated colour is dimmer in measured photons than the matching grey, and yet the eye accepts them as the same brightness. The gap is largest for blues and purples (where it can exceed 40 ΔY) and smallest in the yellow-greens where the eye is already near peak sensitivity. The effect is why a fully saturated phthalo blue tube of paint reads as «bright» despite being measurably dark, and why the HSL model — which has no chroma-to-lightness term — places saturated blues at the same numerical value as pale ones.

gamutMap.title: Gamut Mapping: Clipping vs. Chroma Preserved
gamutMap.hint: Adjust Hue, Lightness, and Chroma · see how out-of-gamut colors map
gamutMap.canvasAria: A 2D plot showing Lightness vs Chroma for the selected Hue. The white curve shows the sRGB gamut boundary. A red dot represents the chosen color, mapping to its clipped and chroma-reduced targets.
gamutMap.cap: When a color falls outside the sRGB triangle, your monitor cannot display it. Relative Colorimetric Clipping clamps each RGB channel independently, which shifts the color's hue and changes its lightness. Chroma Preserved Mapping reduces only the chroma (vividness) horizontally in the OKLCH space, keeping the lightness and hue constant. The white curve in the graph shows the boundary of sRGB for the chosen Hue. Notice how clipping shifts the coordinates, while mapping slides them directly onto the boundary.

note.label: The color you will not see
note.body: We can now place a color, and measure it, and trust the measurement. And yet that measurement is still not the color you will see — because the eye never judges a color alone. It judges every color by the colors around it. Chapter Eight is about that betrayal.

ch8.title: The Interaction of Color
ch8.standfirst: No color is ever seen alone.
ch8.leadIn: Josef Albers taught color for forty years — at the Bauhaus, at Black Mountain, at Yale — and in 1963 he set the whole of it down in a book called Interaction of Color. Its first principle is also its hardest: color is the most relative medium in art. A color is never seen as it is. It is always seen in the company of whatever surrounds it, and that company changes it.
ch8.heringIntro: Behind that relativity lies a piece of wiring. Chapter Two showed three cones; what was not yet shown is that the brain immediately recodes their signals into opposite pairs — red against green, yellow against blue. The German physiologist Ewald Hering proposed the scheme in 1892, against Helmholtz's three-receptor consensus, and he was right: both are true, layered. The hardest prediction of his theory is that the two members of a pair cannot coexist in the same patch of vision. There is no such thing as a reddish-green, or a bluish-yellow, the way there is a reddish-blue (violet) or a yellowish-green (chartreuse). Below is the cancellation experiment that lets you feel that constraint with your own eyes.
ch8.proveBody: The two squares at the centre of the panels below are painted in a single color — the very same color, the same three numbers. Set their surroundings, and watch them refuse to agree.
ch8.simContrastBody: This is simultaneous contrast, named by the chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul in 1839, when he was sent to explain why the same wool looked wrong in different weaves at the Gobelins tapestry works. The eye grades every color against its surroundings: a color on a darker ground lifts, the very same color on a lighter ground sinks — as the two centre squares above have just shown. Contrast works in hue as well as in lightness — a grey set beside orange cools toward blue, beside blue it warms toward orange — but the lesson is single: the eye reports differences, never absolutes.
ch8.bezoldBody: The influence can spread, too. In the Bezold effect — noticed by the meteorologist Wilhelm von Bezold while designing rugs — changing one color in a repeating pattern shifts the hue and tone of the whole design at once, as that single color carries through every shape it touches.
ch8.neonIntro: An extreme case of that spreading is neon color spreading, first described by Dario Varin and Harrie van Tuijl in the 1970s. Where a thin coloured stroke crosses a contour of a different colour on a dark ground, the eye fills the interior of the contour with the crossing colour as though a tinted disc had been laid behind it. The colour is in the strokes only — the rest is invented.
ch8.successiveBody: That ghost is a successive contrast, an afterimage. The eye does not merely count its three cones; at the next stage it sets them against one another in opposed pairs — red against green, blue against yellow. Hold a color still on one patch of the retina and the cones that carry it slowly tire; when the color is withdrawn, its worn-out side falls quiet while the opposing one answers unopposed, and you see the complement, painted upon nothing at all. It is the same opposition that sets complementary colors buzzing when they are placed side by side: the eye was built to answer contrast, and it cannot be told to stop.
ch8.landIntro: If that sounds like the eye is doing more than reading light, it is. In 1959 the engineer and Polaroid founder Edwin Land showed it could do something almost ridiculous: from two black-and-white photographs — one taken through a long-wavelength filter, one through a shorter — projected back through a red filter and a white lamp, respectively, the visual system reconstructs an apparently full colour image. There is no green light, no blue light, anywhere in the room. The brain manufactures the missing hues from the spatial structure of the two records, edges and ratios doing the work that pure wavelength cannot. Land called the underlying account the retinex theory, for retina and cortex. The simulation below lets you stand inside that experiment.
ch8.hering: Behind all of these effects is a structural fact about the visual pathway, first proposed by Ewald Hering in 1892: the signal that leaves the retina is not a list of three cone activations, but a difference. The output of L and M cones is subtracted to form a red–green channel; the output of S is subtracted from the sum of L and M to form a yellow–blue channel; and L+M+S becomes the brightness channel. Inside each opponent channel, the two poles cannot coexist — there is no such thing as a reddish-green or a yellowish-blue, the way there is a reddish-orange. The dial below lets you push a sample colour along the two opponent axes and watch the nervous system's "two-poles-only" rule do its work.
ch8.goethe: Goethe, two centuries before Hering, had already collected a catalogue of phenomena the eye produced of its own accord. The most beautiful was the coloured shadow: light a white wall with two lamps, one of any spectral colour, the other neutral white, and the shadow cast by a finger or pencil in front of the coloured lamp is not grey but vivid in the complement of the lamp's colour. A red lamp casts a cyan shadow on a white wall, an orange lamp a blue one, a yellow lamp a violet one. The physics is uncontroversial — only the white lamp's light reaches the shadow, and that light contains the complement of the coloured lamp's hue in roughly equal measure to everything else — but the saturation of the perceived colour goes far beyond what the physical mixture predicts. The nervous system, having decided that the room is «the colour of the coloured lamp», treats anything dimmer as a deviation in the opposite direction, and renders it accordingly.
ch8.assim: One last reverse. Albers and Bezold showed that two colours in close geometric contact push each other apart in perception (simultaneous contrast). At very fine spatial scales — thin stripes, dot patterns, small textures — the same two colours do the opposite: they pull each other together, blending in the eye until each is taken to be a little more like its neighbour. This is color assimilation, or the Bezold effect, and it is the reason a thin red line on a green field looks more like a red-orange line on a teal field, and a stamp printed in magenta dots on yellow paper reads as a warm orange from a metre away. The threshold at which contrast flips to assimilation is a matter of spatial frequency — how many edges per degree of visual angle — and it shifts with viewing distance and lighting.

hering.title: Hering's opponent channels
hering.hint: Push along red↔green and yellow↔blue · the channels cancel at zero
hering.stageAria: A grey reference patch on the left and a coloured target patch on the right. Two opposed sliders push the target along the red-green axis and the yellow-blue axis. At zero on both sliders the target is neutral grey; pushing one axis colours the patch in that direction; setting opposite signs on the two axes produces familiar in-between colours (orange, teal, magenta, chartreuse); pushing the same axis to its limit and the opposite axis to its limit produces no muddier middle, only the dominant pole — the system refuses to render a reddish-green.
hering.ariaRG: Red to green opponent channel, negative is green, positive is red
hering.ariaYB: Yellow to blue opponent channel, negative is blue, positive is yellow
hering.cap: Hering's opponent-process theory (1892) replaced Helmholtz's three-cone model as the explanation of what the eye ships upstream. The two are not in conflict; the retina has three receptors (Helmholtz), but the retinal ganglion cells combine and subtract their outputs into three opponent channels (Hering) before the signal leaves the eye. The colour you see is the brain's reading of those differences. The familiar names of impossible colours — reddish-green, yellowish-blue — describe combinations the opponent channels cannot encode; the names refer to nothing in the world, only to the rules of the channel.

albers.title: One Color, Two Colors
albers.hint: Adjust the grounds, then prove the centres equal
albers.ariaPattern: Pattern frequency on the surrounds: zero is solid, higher is finer stripes
albers.verdict: Both centre squares hold the very same color.
albers.cap: The wider the gap between the two grounds, the more the single centre color splits in two — sinking dark against the light ground, lifting pale against the dark. The eye is grading it against its surroundings, never reading it on its own. Turn the lower slider for a second lesson: at wide stripes the contrast around the centre sharpens, but as the stripes go fine the eye stops separating them from the field — the surround averages itself, and the centre assimilates toward the stripe colour. Wilhelm von Bezold noticed the effect in 1874.

neon.title: Neon Color Spreading
neon.svgAria: A dark field crossed by a thin white grid. At the central intersections, a single coloured stroke replaces the white. The eye sees a tinted disc filling the central region, although only the crossing strokes carry colour.
neon.note: The dotted ring, when shown, marks where the eye paints a tinted disc that has no physical paint in it — only the few coloured strokes inside that ring carry pigment.
neon.cap: Where the Albers panels above showed neighbouring colours pushing each other apart (simultaneous contrast) and fine stripes melting into the field (Bezold assimilation), this figure is assimilation pushed to its limit. The visual system, primed by the closed grid to expect a continuous surface, paints the inside of the "ring" with the colour it finds at its boundary — even when almost the entire inside is bare dark ground. The same machinery underlies coloured shadows, watercolour effects, and almost every designer's reach for restraint: show a colour at the edge, the interior fills itself in.

afterimage.title: The Afterimage
afterimage.hint: Stare at the cross, then look away
afterimage.cap: Hold your gaze on the small cross for twenty seconds or so — do not let it wander — then press Look away. On the bare grey field, the shape returns as a ghost, painted in its complement.

land.title: Land's Two-Color Projection
land.hint: Hover the output to read a pixel's R, G, B
land.outLabel: Land's projection · what the room shows
land.origAria: The original colour scene that the long-wave and short-wave records were taken from
land.outAria: The simulated output of Land's two-projector setup. Hover or focus to read the actual R, G, B values of any pixel — they will be much simpler than the colour you perceive.
land.cap: The left panel shows the colour scene the two black-and-white slides were "taken" from. The right panel is what a viewer in Land's lecture room would actually see: only two physical lights, a red and a white, modulated by the two grayscale records. Hover or focus the right panel and read the verdict — pixels that look orange, yellow, or even green-tinted have no green light and no blue light in them at all. Their R, G, B numbers will show this plainly. The colours you see anyway are the visual system filling in, from edges and surround context, the hues the room never sent. The effect is strongest on a calibrated screen in a dim room; under bright office light it weakens but is still visible on the warm side of the spectrum.

goethe.title: Goethe's coloured shadow
goethe.hint: Pick a lamp colour · watch the shadow take on its complement
goethe.stageAria: A white wall lit by two lamps. The left lamp is white; the right lamp is a coloured lamp whose hue the reader chooses. A small figure casts two shadows on the wall: the shadow on the left, away from the white lamp, falls in the light of the coloured lamp and is dim and tinted by it; the shadow on the right, away from the coloured lamp, falls in white light alone and looks neutral grey at first — but is perceived strongly as the complement of the coloured lamp's hue.
goethe.ariaHue: Hue of the coloured lamp on the right, 0 to 360 degrees
goethe.cap: Two lamps, one white, one coloured. The shadow on the side away from the white lamp is lit only by the coloured lamp, and shows that colour faintly. The shadow on the side away from the coloured lamp is lit only by white — but the visual system, having read the dominant lamp colour as the room's white point, treats anything else as a deviation toward the complement and renders the right-hand shadow in vivid cyan, blue, violet, or chartreuse, according to the choice of lamp. The effect was the first item in Goethe's Theory of Colours (1810), and is still the most direct demonstration of the opponent-channel rule working in the wild.

assim.title: Color assimilation: when contrast becomes blending
assim.hint: Make the stripes finer · watch contrast invert into blending
assim.stageAria: A square field divided horizontally into a top half and a bottom half. Each half contains the same coloured target stripes; the top half is overlaid with thin black grid lines and the bottom half with thin white grid lines. As the stripe spacing narrows, the coloured target in the top half appears to darken and the same target in the bottom half appears to lighten — the visual system has begun to mix the surround into the target instead of contrasting against it.
assim.cap: The same orange target in two halves of the field. Thin black lines overlaid on the top half pull the target toward darkness; thin white lines on the bottom half pull it toward light. Narrow the lines and the assimilation strengthens until, near the resolution limit of the eye, the target on the top half is darker than its physical RGB value and the target on the bottom half is lighter — neither change is in the pixel data, both are in the eye. The phenomenon was studied carefully by Wilhelm von Bezold in 1874 and is the inverse of the simultaneous contrast Albers built his pedagogy around.

note.label: Color that has to work
note.body: If the measured color is never quite the color that is seen, then anyone who builds with color for other people — a sign, an interface, a page — is working on shifting ground. The last full chapter is about standing on it regardless: color that stays legible, and stays kind, for every eye.

ch9.title: Color in Practice
ch9.standfirst: Color that has to be read by everyone.
ch9.leadIn: Eight chapters have gone to how color behaves. This one is about a duty. When color is asked to carry meaning — on a sign, a screen, a page — it has to reach every reader, not only the well-lit and the typically sighted. Two demands cover most of it: color must be legible, and it must be inclusive.
ch9.contrastBody: Legibility is, above all else, a matter of contrast. Text can be read when it is light enough — or dark enough — against its background, and that "enough" can be put to a single number. Set a text color and a background below.
ch9.wcagBody: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines set the thresholds the badges test. Body text needs a ratio of at least 4.5 : 1 to pass at the ordinary level, AA; large text — around 24 pixels, or 19 if bold — needs only 3 : 1; the strict level, AAA, asks 7 : 1 of body text. These are not bureaucratic numbers. They are the margin between a sentence that is read and one that is squinted at, given up on, or never noticed at all — by a reader in sunlight, on a dying screen, or simply with older eyes.
ch9.apcaBody: The figure also reads a newer number beside the ratio: APCA, the contrast measure W3C is preparing for the next version of the guidelines. Where WCAG counts only the brightness gap, APCA reads the gap as the eye does, and it does not pretend that dark-on-light and light-on-dark are the same problem. Its guidance then attaches different Lc minimums to different sizes and weights of type: body text wants at least Lc 75, large or bold text 60, headings 45, and merely visible non-text 30. The scale (signed, with positive for darker text on lighter ground) runs to about a hundred at the extreme.
ch9.inclusionBody: The second demand is inclusion. Among people of European descent, roughly one man in twelve and one woman in two hundred — the rate shifts with ancestry — meet color with a different set of cones than this essay has so far assumed. Most often a single cone type is shifted or absent: protanopia and deuteranopia weaken the line between red and green; the rarer tritanopia blurs blue against yellow. The eight colors sent to the screen below never change; what each setting shows is how a different eye would resolve them.
ch9.rulePracticalBody: Watch the red and the green slide toward one muddy tone under protanopia or deuteranopia, and the practical rule writes itself: never let color be the only signal. A red word and a green word, alike in every other respect, are two words a great many readers cannot tell apart. Add a second channel — a shape, a label, an underline, a position — and color becomes a welcome reinforcement rather than a locked door. Color should be the easiest way to read a thing; it must never be the only way.
ch9.balanceBody: One last note before the road ends. A palette is not just three good colours but the shares they take of the page. Designers have long leaned on a rule of thumb: a room, a poster, or a screen reads as balanced when one colour does about sixty per cent of the work, a second around thirty, and the third only about ten. The dominant carries the space; the secondary supports it; the accent draws the eye and then steps back. Give every colour an equal share and the composition loses its centre.

contrast.title: The Contrast Checker
contrast.hint: Pick a text color and a background
contrast.previewSm: Body text — the size most words on a page are set in, and the size that asks the most of contrast.
contrast.cap: The number is the contrast ratio — the lighter color's luminance against the darker's, running from 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (pure black on pure white).

cvd.title: Through Other Eyes
cvd.hint: A simulation — choose a kind of vision
cvd.severityLabel: Severity — anomalous trichromacy to complete dichromacy
cvd.severityAria: Severity, percent — at 0 the simulation is typical vision; intermediate values approximate anomalous trichromacy; 100 models complete dichromacy

cvd.cap: A mathematical approximation. At severity 100 it models complete dichromacy — a missing cone; intermediate severities approximate anomalous trichromacy (a cone shifted rather than absent), the milder and far more common form. No ordinary screen can reproduce the true experience.

Once you're done, check your score and share your Color IQ badge!

note.label: The end of the road
note.body: And that is the essay — from a single wavelength of light to the discipline of a palette that works for every eye. One short chapter remains: not an argument but a reference, the terms of color gathered in a single place.

ch10.title: A Glossary of Color
ch10.standfirst: Every term the essay leaned on, gathered in one place.
ch10.leadIn: Not an argument this time, but a reference. Each term below has its home in one of the nine chapters; the marker beside it points the way. Type in the box to narrow the list.

additiveMixing.name: Additive mixing
additiveMixing.def: Making color by combining light: begin in darkness and add. Red, green, and blue light together make white — the logic of screens and stage lights.

afterimage.name: Afterimage
afterimage.def: The colored ghost seen once a color is withdrawn — its complement, produced as the eye's tired opponent channels rebound.

analogous.name: Analogous
analogous.def: A harmony of neighbouring hues, close together on the wheel — one family, quietly at ease.

chroma.name: Chroma
chroma.def: How pure or how muted a color is: its distance from a neutral grey. One of color's three dimensions.

chromaticity.name: Chromaticity
chromaticity.def: A color's hue and saturation taken together, considered apart from its brightness.

cie1931.name: CIE 1931
cie1931.def: The colorimetric standard built from human color-matching — and the source of the horseshoe chromaticity diagram.

cmyk.name: CMYK
cmyk.def: Cyan, magenta, yellow, and key black: the subtractive primaries of print.

colorSpace.name: Color space
colorSpace.def: A coordinate system for color — a way to fix any color with a few numbers. RGB, HSL, and OKLCH are color spaces.

cvd.name: Color vision deficiency
cvd.def: A difference in the cones — usually one missing or shifted — that weakens the line between certain colors, most often red and green.

colorWheel.name: Color wheel
colorWheel.def: The spectral line bent into a ring, its two ends joined through the non-spectral purples. An invention, and a useful one.

complementary.name: Complementary
complementary.def: Two colors facing each other across the wheel — the sharpest contrast a pair can hold.

coneCell.name: Cone cell
coneCell.def: One of the retina's three color receptors — short, medium, and long (S, M, L). Their three signals are the whole of color seen by daylight.

contrastRatio.name: Contrast ratio
contrastRatio.def: The luminance ratio of two colors, from 1:1 to 21:1. WCAG asks at least 4.5:1 of body text.

gamut.name: Gamut
gamut.def: The set of colors a given device or space can actually produce — always smaller than all the eye can see.

harmony.name: Harmony
harmony.def: Colors that belong together, set by simple geometry on the wheel: a grammar for combining color, not a law.

hsl.name: HSL
hsl.def: Hue, Saturation, Lightness — an intuitive color space, though its lightness is not perceptually even.

hue.name: Hue
hue.def: The quality a color word names — red, green, blue — and the dimension that runs around the wheel.

metamerism.name: Metamerism
metamerism.def: Two physically different lights that fill the three cones to the same levels, and so look identical though they are not.

munsell.name: Munsell
munsell.def: Albert Munsell's color-order system, around 1905 — the first mapped by measurement, placing every color by hue, value, and chroma.

oklch.name: OKLCH
oklch.def: A perceptually uniform color space (Björn Ottosson, 2020) where equal steps look equal — the cylindrical form of OKLab, now part of CSS.

opponentProcess.name: Opponent process
opponentProcess.def: The second stage of color vision: the cone signals set against one another in pairs — red against green, blue against yellow.

primaryColors.name: Primary colors
primaryColors.def: A chosen set from which others are mixed. There is no single true set: RGB for light, CMY for pigment, RYB for the painter.

rgb.name: RGB
rgb.def: Red, Green, Blue: the additive primaries of light, and the color space native to screens.

saturation.name: Saturation
saturation.def: How vivid or how washed a color looks; in screen and everyday use, the working cousin of chroma.

simultaneousContrast.name: Simultaneous contrast
simultaneousContrast.def: The shift a color undergoes on account of its neighbours. The eye grades every color against its surroundings.

spectralColor.name: Spectral color
spectralColor.def: A color carried by a single wavelength of light. Magenta is not one — it has no wavelength of its own.

subtractiveMixing.name: Subtractive mixing
subtractiveMixing.def: Making color by removing light: begin with white and take away. Each pigment absorbs part of the spectrum.

tintShadeTone.name: Tint, shade, and tone
tintShadeTone.def: Three ways to move a color: a tint adds white, a shade adds black, a tone adds grey.

trichromatic.name: Trichromatic vision
trichromatic.def: Human color sight: three cone types, and color assembled by the brain from the ratio of their three signals.

value.name: Value
value.def: How light or dark a color is — its place on the road from black to white. One of color's three dimensions.

visibleSpectrum.name: Visible spectrum
visibleSpectrum.def: The narrow band of wavelengths the eye can catch, roughly 380 nanometres (violet) to 700 (red).

wavelength.name: Wavelength
wavelength.def: The length of one cycle of a light wave, in nanometres — the stimulus the cones absorb in differing proportions to make the three signals the brain reads as color.

note.label: The last word
note.body: And there the argument rests. Color began as a fact of physics and ends as a discipline of care — and across all ten chapters it was never once a property of things. It is an event: a meeting of light, matter, and a looking eye, and it lasts exactly as long as the looking does.

ch12.title: Pigments
ch12.standfirst: The history of color is the history of pigments. And pigments are made of chemistry, trade, and power.
ch12.leadIn: A color, until the late nineteenth century, was almost always a thing — a stone ground to powder, a shellfish boiled until it bled, a beetle scraped from a cactus. The history of color, before the chemists arrived, is mostly the history of finding rare substances in inconvenient places and shipping them at great expense across the world.
ch12.earth: The oldest pigments are the most generous ones — the ones the earth already had ground up and lying about. The cave painters of Lascaux, seventeen thousand years ago, used yellow ochre and red ochre — iron oxides — that they could pick up from the ground around the cave mouth. Burnt the same ochre and it darkened to brown; heated it to red glow and it became more saturated still. Vermilion — the red of cinnabar, mercury sulfide — was found in red veins and pounded to a fine powder, the most expensive non-blue pigment of the ancient world. Malachite for green, azurite for blue: both were copper carbonates, both mined where copper was mined, both stable enough to last for millennia on a tomb wall.
ch12.ultramarine: Of all the pigments before synthesis, the most extraordinary was ultramarine — the blue of lapis lazuli, a stone mined in only one place in the world: the Sar-i Sang valley in the mountains of what is now north-eastern Afghanistan. Extracted there from at least the sixth millennium BCE, it travelled by camel and ship to Venice, where it was further refined by being kneaded with wax and ash, and from Venice it dispersed to the workshops of Renaissance Europe. By the fifteenth century it cost more, gram for gram, than gold. The blue of Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, the blue of every Madonna's robe in early Italian painting, the blue of the lapis ornaments of Tutankhamun's coffin — all came from one Afghan valley. The name ultramarine means simply from beyond the sea.
ch12.tyrian: The story repeats with Tyrian purple, the dye reserved for Roman emperors. It came from a Mediterranean sea snail (Murex brandaris), one of those organisms that produces a tiny amount of a precious substance under just the right conditions of stress. The Phoenicians of Tyre had perfected its extraction by the second millennium BCE. A single gram of dye required around twelve thousand snails, harvested and crushed and left to ferment in vats whose stench, the historians tell us, was unbearable for a city block in every direction. A pound of dyed wool cost roughly its weight in silver. The colour itself was not quite purple in the modern sense — a deep blood-red with an iridescent violet sheen — but it was the most expensive colour anyone had ever produced, and so by social convention it became the colour of power.
ch12.indian: Other pigments came with stranger biographies. Indian yellow, used in European painting from the seventeenth century to the early twentieth, was made — according to the surviving accounts — from the dried urine of cattle in rural Bengal that had been fed exclusively on mango leaves. The mango diet starved the cows and yielded a small daily supply of a brilliant, glowing yellow whose chemistry (a magnesium salt of euxanthic acid) European chemists worked out only in the 1880s. It was banned, on animal-welfare grounds, in 1908. Modern Indian yellow is a synthetic; the old jars in museum drawers are sometimes the last of the cow-given kind.
ch12.mummy: Stranger still: mummy brown. From at least the sixteenth century, European apothecaries imported powdered Egyptian mummies — human and feline — as a pigment, a deep semi-transparent brown popular for shadows and skin tones. The painters of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, in the 1860s, used it without thinking until Edward Burne-Jones learned where it came from and, the story goes, took the tube of mummy brown out into the garden and buried it. Production trailed off through the twentieth century; the last commercial tube was sold by Roberson's of London in 1964, when, they explained politely, they had run out of mummies.
ch12.mauve: Everything changed in 1856. An eighteen-year-old chemistry student in London, William Henry Perkin, was trying to synthesise quinine for malaria treatment, failed, and produced instead a dark sludge that, when he washed it out of the flask, stained the cloth a vivid purple. The purple was unfading, unbleaching, and could be made from coal tar — a waste product of the gas industry, then piling up in vast and useless heaps. Perkin patented the dye, named it mauve, opened a factory, and at twenty-one was rich. The discovery launched the synthetic dye industry; within forty years almost every pigment a painter or dyer used was a coal-tar derivative, and the companies founded to make them — BASF, Hoechst, Bayer, Agfa — became the chemical giants of the twentieth century. The age of natural pigments was, suddenly, over.
ch12.cadmium: What replaced it was a flood of synthetic colours, each more saturated and lightfast than the rare substance it replaced. Cadmium yellow and cadmium red — discovered 1817, made commercially from the 1840s — gave painters from Monet to Van Gogh their fierce, glowing oranges and yellows. Cobalt blue (1802) replaced ultramarine for everyday use; cerulean (1860) joined it. Titanium white, commercialised in 1916, replaced the lead white that had poisoned painters for two thousand years — Vermeer, Caravaggio, and many others died young, with lead poisoning long suspected as a major cause — the very white that made their highlights possible. The new whites were, for the first time, safe to use. The new chemistry was no longer a matter of finding the rare; it was a matter of designing the molecule.
ch12.vantablack: And the cycle continues. In 2014 the firm Surrey NanoSystems announced Vantablack, a coating of vertically aligned carbon nanotubes that absorbs 99.965 % of visible light — the blackest substance ever measured. The British sculptor Anish Kapoor secured an exclusive licence to it for artistic use, and a small art-world war broke out over whether a single artist should own a colour. The painter Stuart Semple released a competing pigment called Pinkest Pink with a licence forbidding Kapoor from buying it. Kapoor bought some anyway. The exchanges have continued, comic and serious in turn, but the underlying point is older than they think — every age that has invented a new colour has fought, at least for a while, over who is allowed to use it.
ch12.astm: By the late twentieth century the chemistry was settled enough that someone had to invent a label for it. The American Society for Testing and Materials — ASTM, founded in 1898 — issued D4303 in 1982, a procedure for measuring a pigment's lightfastness: paint a strip, expose half of it to a year of sunlight, measure the colour shift, and grade the result from I (Excellent) through V (Fugitive). Museum-grade work uses I and II only. A second standard, D4236, was added in 1988 after the U.S. Labelling of Hazardous Art Materials Act required chronic-hazard warnings on every tube of paint sold to amateurs — cadmium for cancer risk, lead for neurotoxicity, cobalt for both. The phrase «Conforms to ASTM D4236» on a tube means a toxicologist has read the formulation. The third element is the Colour Index code — PR108 for Cadmium Red, PB29 for Ultramarine, PG7 for Phthalo Green — a three-character designation maintained by the Society of Dyers and Colourists since 1925 that lets a chemist know exactly which compound is in the tube regardless of what the marketing department called it. Hold a modern paint tube up to the light and you can read its physics, its danger, and its history in less than a square centimetre.
ch12.closing: The chemists won the argument, by and large. A painter today can buy a tube of every colour an Old Master would have killed for, for the price of lunch. But the older logic of colour — that a hue was a substance, that a substance was a place, and that a place gave you a politics — still lives in the names. Naples yellow came from Vesuvius. Sienna came from Siena. Indian yellow, however briefly we still use it, points to the Bengal where it once was made. The synthetic age has freed us from the substance, but the colour-name carries the substance's ghost.
ch12.fading: The lightfastness rating is not a slogan but a number, and the slider below lets you accelerate the measurement. Six historical pigments are painted onto a strip; the slider stands for how many decades of museum-light exposure (about 150 lux for eight hours a day, the standard for the Louvre's loaned works) the strip has endured. Pigments with ASTM I and II ratings barely move. Pigments rated III, IV, V — the historical fugitive colours like alizarin crimson, indian yellow, mauveine, dragon's blood — visibly drift toward grey within the first century. Real fading is more complex and depends on humidity, binder, and trace impurities; this is a cartoon, but it is a cartoon with the right rank order.
