timeline.cap: Each dot marks the approximate date a pigment entered widespread use; its colour is the pigment itself, drawn at typical saturation. The pre-1850 pigments are natural — earths, stones, plants, shellfish. After 1856, the synthetic age opens with Perkin's mauve, and almost every later pigment is a coal-tar derivative, a metal oxide, or a designed organic compound. The cluster of names compresses fifty thousand years of pigment history into a single, walkable line.

tube.title: A modern paint tube, decoded
tube.hint: Six labels · six histories on a square inch of metal
tube.imgAlt: A photograph of a real paint tube of Cadmium Red Medium lying on a wooden workbench. The label, printed in black on a cream rectangular field, shows six pieces of information: the colour name 'Cadmium Red Medium' top centre, the series number 'Series 4' top right, the Colour Index pigment code 'PR108' middle left, the lightfastness rating 'ASTM Lightfastness I' middle centre, the genuineness marker 'Hue vs Genuine' middle right, and the safety conformance 'Conforms to ASTM D4236' along the bottom. To the left of the label sits a small red colour swatch — a direct sample of the pigment the tube contains.
tube.name: Cadmium Red Medium
tube.nameNote: The commercial name. Medium places this colour between the cooler Light and the warmer Deep within the same pigment family — the manufacturer shifts the hue by sintering temperature, not by adding other pigments.
tube.seriesNote: The price tier. Series 4 is among the most expensive — the pigment here is genuine cadmium sulfoselenide, not a hue substitute. Manufacturers price tubes by raw material cost from series 1 (earth pigments) through 7 or 8 (cobalt, cadmium, rare modern synthetics).
tube.ciNote: PR108 = Pigment Red 108 = cadmium sulfoselenide. The first letter is the colour family (R, Y, B, G, Br, W, Bk, Vi, O, M); the number is the order of discovery within that family. Registered by the Society of Dyers and Colourists since 1925. Two tubes from different brands with the same CI code contain the same pigment.
tube.lfNote: ASTM D4303 rating. I (Excellent) and II (Very Good) are museum-grade — under accelerated one-year sun exposure the colour shift is below the threshold of perception. III is Fair. IV (Poor) and V (Fugitive) bleach visibly within months and should be avoided for any work intended to last.
tube.hueNote: A tube labelled Cadmium Red Hue contains no cadmium — it is a less expensive, less toxic, and usually less opaque substitute that matches the colour. Genuine means the pigment named on the label is in fact present. The two look identical in the squeeze but behave differently in mixes, layers, and over decades.
tube.confNote: ASTM D4236: a U.S. standard requiring chronic-hazard labelling on any art material likely to be inhaled, ingested, or absorbed. The phrase means a toxicologist has reviewed the formulation. Cadmium pigments carry a separate «harmful if swallowed» warning; lead pigments are restricted to professional grades; cobalt pigments require a dust warning.
tube.cap: A paint tube is one of the few consumer products that legally must declare its physical and chemical contents. Read the labels in order and you have the history of the standards themselves: the Colour Index (1925), ASTM D4303 lightfastness (1982), and ASTM D4236 chronic-hazard conformance (1988). The tube is a small monument to a century of trying to make a hazardous, beautiful chemistry safe to teach to a child.

fading.title: A century of museum light
fading.hint: Drag through the decades · watch the fugitive pigments fade
fading.stageAria: A row of six painted pigment swatches: ultramarine (PB29, rated ASTM I), titanium white (PW6, ASTM I), cadmium red (PR108, ASTM I), alizarin crimson (PR83, ASTM III), Indian yellow (PY13, ASTM IV), and mauveine (PV2, ASTM V). A time slider runs from year zero to year one hundred of museum-light exposure. The first three swatches barely change colour. The last three visibly fade — alizarin crimson loses chroma by year twenty, Indian yellow loses both chroma and value by year fifty, mauveine is nearly grey by year eighty.
fading.cap: Six pigments, six lightfastness ratings. Ultramarine, titanium white, and cadmium red (all ASTM I) hold their colour for centuries with no special precautions. Alizarin crimson (PR83, ASTM III) is the classic example of a beautiful pigment a museum will not collect new work in; it darkens and shifts toward brown within a working artist's lifetime. Indian yellow (PY13, IV) and mauveine (PV2, V) are fugitive enough that almost no surviving examples of nineteenth-century works in them look the colour the artist mixed. The exponential here uses the ASTM-grade decay constant; the real curve depends on humidity, binder, oxygen, and a half-dozen trace impurities, but the rank order is right.

note.label: On to the natural side
note.body: Pigments are how we have made colours. The next chapter looks at how nature already made them — without us, and often using machinery we are only beginning to copy.

ch13.title: Nature
ch13.standfirst: Nature makes color in two ways: pigment, or structure. Both work without anyone designing them.
ch13.leadIn: Look at a forest, a coral reef, a flowerbed, a flock of parrots, and the first impression is of a colourist gone mad. Look closer and there are exactly two methods at work, used in different proportions. A leaf, an animal's eye, a brown beetle, a red poppy — these are pigment: a molecule absorbs some wavelengths and reflects the rest. A peacock's tail, a hummingbird's throat, the wing of a morpho butterfly, the surface of a soap bubble — these are structure: not absorption at all, but interference, the way light bends and overlaps in a layer thinner than itself.
ch13.chlorophyll: The most widespread pigment on Earth is chlorophyll, the molecule that makes leaves green. It absorbs most strongly in the red and the blue and reflects the medium wavelengths — green. This is, in some sense, an inefficiency. The sun's peak energy lies in the green; a chlorophyll molecule that absorbed green and reflected red and blue would harvest more light. There is no good account of why the plants ended up with chlorophyll rather than its mirror image. One leading theory is that early purple photosynthetic bacteria, using bacteriorhodopsin, had already taken the green band by the time chlorophyll-based plants evolved; chlorophyll worked with what was left. The Earth is green not because green is best but because, once, it was second.
ch13.melanin: Animal skin, fur, and hair carry a different family of pigments: the melanins. Eumelanin is brown-black, the pigment of dark hair, dark skin, the spots on a leopard. Pheomelanin is reddish-yellow, the pigment of red hair, freckles, and the orange of a tabby cat. The two are produced from the same precursor, tyrosine, and the ratio between them — controlled by a handful of genes — produces almost every variation in human hair colour. Bird feathers, fish scales, and the irises of human eyes use the same two pigments in different proportions. Melanin also absorbs ultraviolet, which is why darker skin protects against sunburn; the pigment is a sunscreen invented several billion years before the chemistry industry got to it.
ch13.carotenoids: The yellows and oranges of fruits, autumn leaves, the egg yolk of a chicken, and the pink of a flamingo are carotenoids — long-chain molecules of which beta-carotene is the most famous. Animals cannot make them; they have to eat them. A flamingo is pink because its diet of brine shrimp and algae is rich in carotenoids; remove the shrimp and the flamingo gradually loses its colour. A canary is yellow for the same reason. Carrots are orange because the plant uses carotene to protect chlorophyll from excess light; we get the colour back when we eat them.
ch13.structural: Pigment is one method. Structural colour is the other, and it is older and stranger. The wing of a Morpho butterfly is brown — under a microscope, the actual chitin is dull brown — but the surface is etched with ridges spaced so that blue light, reflecting off the layers, interferes constructively, and a brilliant iridescent blue results from a pigmentless surface. A peacock's tail uses the same trick at a different scale: the eyespots are not painted, they are structured, the colour produced by thin keratin layers in the feather barbs. Soap films, oil on a wet road, the surface of a CD — all of these are structural colour. Heat or wet or scratch them and the colour vanishes, because what you have damaged is not the molecule but the geometry.
ch13.rayleigh: The biggest structural colour on the planet is the sky. Sunlight is white; the atmosphere scatters short wavelengths (blue) more than long (red), an effect Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt) worked out in 1871. Looking up away from the sun, you see the scattered light: blue. Looking toward the sun at sunset, when the light has travelled through several times as much air to reach you, the blue has been almost entirely scattered out somewhere over the horizon; what arrives is the red that scattered least. Mars, with a thin and dusty atmosphere, has a butterscotch sky at noon and a blue sunset, the opposite of ours, because the dust grains scatter the longer wavelengths more. The sky is not a colour; the sky is a length of air with the sun's light passing through it.
ch13.biolumin: Some animals make their own light. The firefly, the angler-fish, the dinoflagellate plankton that sometimes turn a wave breaking on a beach a luminous blue — all of these use a family of enzymes called luciferases, which catalyse a reaction that releases energy as a photon rather than as heat. Most bioluminescence is in a narrow band of blue-green, a wavelength that travels furthest through sea water; the bioluminescence of land insects has spread into yellow and orange because the air does not impose the same constraint. The light is cold — almost no infrared — and so efficient that engineers have spent the last twenty years trying to copy it for lamps. None has yet succeeded.
ch13.fluorescent: And a colour the human world makes in profusion is almost absent from nature: fluorescence, the absorption of ultraviolet light and the re-emission of the energy at a visible wavelength. A highlighter pen, a fluorescent safety vest, a glowing club bracelet — all are bright in a way nothing in nature quite is, because they emit more visible light than the visible light hitting them would predict; they have been borrowing energy from the UV. A few corals, some scorpions, the gills of certain mushrooms do this faintly; the rest is human chemistry. The dazzle that catches your eye on a roadside vest at dusk is, in evolutionary terms, very new.
ch13.closing: Pigment, structure, scattering, emission. Four methods, used by four billion years of biology and by every chemist since, and they exhaust the inventory of how a thing can be the colour it is. Look at any coloured thing — the page in front of you, the eye that is reading it, the sky behind it — and one of the four is at work.

sky.title: Rayleigh's sky
sky.hint: Drag the sun · noon to sunset
sky.stageAria: A sky simulation: the sun's altitude controls how much atmosphere its light has travelled through. At noon (high sun), short atmospheric path, the sky is blue and the sun is pale yellow. As the sun lowers, the path through the air lengthens, more blue is scattered away, and the sun and the surrounding sky redden toward sunset.
sky.altitudeRangeAria: Sun altitude above the horizon in degrees
sky.cap: Rayleigh scattering of sunlight through Earth's atmosphere, in cartoon form. At noon the sun is high, its light passes through a thin slice of air, and only short (blue) wavelengths scatter strongly — the sky is blue. As the sun descends, its light passes through more and more atmosphere; by the time it reaches you it has lost almost all of its blue to scattering, and the disc of the sun and the sky around it shift toward red. The same atmosphere does both things at once.

fluorescence.title: Fluorescence: the Stokes shift
fluorescence.hint: Switch the lamp · UV in, visible out
fluorescence.stageAria: A dark chamber containing a row of fluorescent samples: a highlighter pen, a coral fragment, a scorpion, and a banknote security fibre. Under ordinary white light the samples look pale; switch the lamp to ultraviolet (365 nm) and the same samples glow vivid green, orange, blue, and pink — emitting visible light from invisible input. The right-hand graph shows a Jablonski diagram: absorption photon arrives at high energy (short wavelength), the molecule relaxes vibrationally, then re-emits at lower energy (longer wavelength) — the Stokes shift.
fluorescence.cap: A schematic Stokes shift. A high-energy photon (short wavelength, here ultraviolet at 365 nm) is absorbed by a molecule and lifts an electron to a vibrationally excited state. The electron sheds a little energy to the lattice as heat, falls to the lowest excited level, and only then emits a photon — which is necessarily of lower energy and longer wavelength than the one that arrived. The visible emission you see (the green of a highlighter, the orange of a coral) is the difference. The phenomenon was named for George Gabriel Stokes, who described it in 1852. It is why blacklight posters glow and why laundry detergents add fluorescent whiteners that absorb UV and emit blue — the shirt looks more white than white.

note.label: To the screens we built
note.body: Chapters 11–13 looked at how a colour comes to be named, made, and grown. The last chapter turns to where most of you reading this are actually looking — a calibrated rectangle of light a few inches across — and asks what to look for when you choose one.

ch14.title: Practice
ch14.standfirst: The screen is the last surface a colour reaches. It is also the one that lies the most about itself.
ch14.leadIn: If you make things with colour — websites, photographs, films, posters, books, branded objects — you are eventually paying for a screen to look at them on. The shop will sell you ten of them at ten different prices and the labels on the boxes are not always straightforward. This chapter is a reader's guide to the labels, and a short tour of the working pipelines (web, print, photography, cinema) that colour passes through on its way from the eye to the world and back.
ch14.monitorSpecs: The single most consequential number on a monitor spec sheet is gamut coverage, given as a percentage of one or more standard colour spaces. 99 % sRGB means the screen can produce 99 % of the colours in the standard web colour space — the bare minimum for any colour work. 95 % DCI-P3 (or Display P3, Apple's variant) means the screen reaches a wider gamut used in cinema and on modern phones — the figure to look for if you edit photographs or video. 99 % Adobe RGB is a third standard, slightly narrower than P3 in the reds and wider in the greens, preferred by people who print to CMYK. A screen with all three above 95 % is genuinely wide-gamut; one that quotes only an sRGB number is not.
ch14.deltaE: After gamut comes accuracy. The number to look for is ΔE (delta-E), the perceptual distance between the colour the screen is asked to display and the colour it actually displays, averaged across many test patches. ΔE under 2 is invisibly accurate; under 1 is laboratory-grade. ΔE under 3 is fine for most design work; above 5 begins to look obviously off. A consumer monitor without a quoted ΔE has not been measured and probably should not be trusted for colour work.
ch14.panel: The panel technology determines viewing angle, contrast, and motion. IPS (in-plane switching) panels have the widest viewing angles and the most accurate colour; almost every colour-work monitor is IPS. OLED panels have perfect blacks (each pixel is its own light source and can switch off completely), the highest contrast, and the most saturated colours, but are vulnerable to burn-in if static UI is shown for long periods. VA panels have higher contrast than IPS but narrower viewing angles. TN panels are the cheapest, the fastest, and the worst at colour — fine for office work and competitive gaming, not for design.
ch14.depth: Bit depth controls how many gradations of each colour the screen can show. An 8-bit panel shows 256 levels per channel, or 16.7 million colours total — enough for most work, but gradients can show visible banding. 8-bit + FRC (frame-rate control) cheats its way to 10-bit by rapidly flickering between two adjacent levels — good enough that most viewers will not see the difference. True 10-bit shows 1.07 billion colours and is the standard for HDR video and serious photo retouching. Almost every screen that quotes "10-bit" in 2024–6 is 8-bit + FRC; the label rarely says which.
ch14.hdr: HDR (high dynamic range) is a bundle of features: wider gamut, higher peak brightness, deeper blacks, often 10-bit colour. The DisplayHDR certification levels (HDR400, HDR600, HDR1000) state the peak brightness in nits; HDR400 is, despite its name, barely HDR — true HDR begins at HDR600 with local dimming, and the most spectacular content needs HDR1000 or above. For desktop work, HDR mostly matters if you grade video; for office work it can be turned off and forgotten.
ch14.calibration: No screen, however expensive, ships colour-accurate. Calibration — a one-time, hour-long procedure using a colorimeter (X-Rite i1Display, Datacolor SpyderX, around $200) — measures the colour the screen actually produces and writes a correction profile. Many high-end monitors ship pre-calibrated with a Pantone or Calman certificate; a few include hardware calibration that adjusts the panel's LUT directly rather than the operating system's. If you cannot or will not calibrate, buy a pre-calibrated screen.
ch14.icc: Across the entire pipeline, an ICC profile — a small file that describes a device's colour behaviour — keeps the colours honest as they move from camera to monitor to printer. The camera tags its RAW with the colour space it used. The image editor reads the tag, converts to the monitor's profile for display, and to the printer's profile for export. A web browser does the same, lazily, with the sRGB profile assumed. If anything in the chain is missing or wrong, the colour shifts — usually in a way you only see when the final piece reaches its destination. The single largest improvement most working colour pipelines could make is to have every device profiled and to assume nothing.
ch14.closing: There is no perfect screen; there is only the screen accurate enough for the work you do. A web designer needs 99 % sRGB and a calibrated ΔE under 2. A photo retoucher needs that plus 95 % Adobe RGB or P3, 10-bit colour, and a Pantone certification. A video colourist needs all of the above plus HDR1000 and a reference monitor. A casual reader of this essay can use any screen, properly viewed in a room with light no stronger than what they would read a paper book by — which is the colour-management trick the rest of the chapter forgets to mention.

note.label: End of practice
note.body: Fourteen chapters have looked at colour from its source to its surface. The Chronology that follows is the spine of dates the whole book hangs on; the Coda is a small palette generator that runs everything you have just read. Open them in any order — the book is, finally, yours.

ch11.title: Names
ch11.standfirst: Color is universal. Its names are made.
ch11.leadIn: Ten chapters have looked at color through physics, optics, perception, geometry, and practice. One more is owed, and a quieter one. The chapters so far treat color as something to be observed; this one asks what we mean when we name it. A hummingbird's throat is the same wavelength to every retina that can resolve it, but the word for that color — iridescent, gorget, fuchsia, 깃털색 — is made by the language doing the looking.
ch11.homer: In 1858, William Gladstone, a serious classical scholar and the future British Prime Minister, sat down with Homer and noticed something strange. The Iliad and Odyssey, in their thousands of lines, almost never name a color the way a modern reader would expect. The sea was oinops — wine-dark, or wine-faced. Sheep were violet. Honey was green. There was no separate word for blue at all, and the sky was, of all things, bronze. Gladstone concluded that the Greeks had defective color vision. He was wrong about the cause. What he had stumbled on was the more interesting fact: ancient Greek had not yet, in 800 BCE, divided the optical world the way English did in 1858.
ch11.berlinKay: A century later, in 1969, the Berkeley anthropologists Brent Berlin and Paul Kay surveyed a hundred languages and noticed a pattern. Languages do not name colors in random order. They acquire color words in a near-fixed sequence. First, almost always, comes a pair: dark and light — read these onto English as black and white, but the words were once broader. The third color is red. The fourth is either yellow or green. Blue comes fifth, brown sixth, then purple, pink, orange, and grey in any order. The Greek of Homer's day, Berlin and Kay would argue, sat at stage three or four — it had black, white, red, and a barely-separated green-yellow, but had not yet split blue from green. The category covers things English calls forest, sea, sky, and the grey-blue of metal — all the things Homer called bronze, violet, and wine.
ch11.japanese: Japanese carries a smaller version of the same fault line. Aoi — usually translated as blue — historically covered everything we would call blue and most of what we would call green, and in some compounds it still does. The traffic signal that says go in Japan is officially aoi and is a noticeably blue-green, because when traffic signals arrived they had to fit into the existing word and the word pulled the color toward itself rather than the other way around. Aoba — aoi leaves — means the leaves of spring, green to any English-speaking eye. The split between aoi (blue-green) and midori (specifically green) is a twentieth-century import, and a partial one.
ch11.russian: Russian goes the other way and splits English's single blue in two. Siniy is the deep, saturated blue of a clear sky at midday. Goluboy is the pale, sky-near-the-horizon blue. To a Russian speaker, these are two different basic colors as distinct as English's blue and red, not two shades of the same word. A study by Jonathan Winawer and colleagues in 2007 showed that Russian speakers, asked to pick a matching shade from a row, were measurably faster at the boundary between siniy and goluboy than English speakers were at any boundary inside blue. The language had given the eye a faster question.
ch11.korean: Korean carries an older system that maps color onto direction. The obangsaek, the five directional colors, are cheong (blue, east), baek (white, west), jeok (red, south), heuk (black, north), and hwang (yellow, centre). The saekdong sleeves of a child's New Year coat — striped in green, red, yellow, blue, and white — are not chosen for prettiness but for the five directions arrayed across the cloth. The system is older than the language's modern color words, and the modern words still carry the older logic underneath: cheong is the color of blue and green together, the direction-color of the east, of spring, of the wood element. The split between blue and green entered Korean later; cheong persists as the older, broader word.
ch11.pirahã: The Pirahã of the Amazon basin — the subject of much linguistic argument since Daniel Everett's fieldwork of the 1980s — do not name colors with single words at all. The closest renderings are biísai (blood-like, for red), xahoasai (blackish, for dark), and kohoaibíísai (like a yellow-tailed bird) — descriptions, not names. Whether this means the Pirahã see color differently is the question Berlin and Kay's work asks most sharply. The answer, increasingly, is no — the eye is the same; the language has simply not yet decided to mint a separate word.
ch11.iscc: Standardisation tried to catch up. In 1955 the Inter-Society Color Council and the U.S. National Bureau of Standards jointly published the ISCC-NBS Method of Designating Colors, a vocabulary of 267 named regions of color space — from vivid red and brilliant pink through moderate olive brown to dark greenish gray — each tied to a specific block of Munsell coordinates so that a name finally meant something measurable. The system never quite displaced everyday usage outside government laboratories and crayon manufacturers, but it remains the only attempt in English to give every nameable color a name and a definition at once.
ch11.newNames: And language is still minting them. In 2014 the British artist Anish Kapoor secured exclusive artistic-use rights to Vantablack, a coating that absorbs 99.965 % of visible light, and the colour acquired its first owner. The internet replied with Stuart Semple's Pink, sold to anyone except Kapoor, and a small war was fought over the name of a black none of us could touch. Millennial pink — a peach-leaning pink that swept design between roughly 2014 and 2019 — was named into being by a magazine writer before the color itself had finished settling. Klein blue, the patented ultramarine of Yves Klein, was the first color to be claimed by a person rather than a place or a plant. Every age has added its words; ours has just made the wording faster.
ch11.closing: The chapters that came before this one looked at color as a property of light and a labor of the eye. This one is for the third party, the one Homer did not have words for: the language. A color exists at the meeting of three things — what reflects, what receives, and what is named. Move any one of them and the color, in the only sense that matters to a sentence, moves.

stages.cap: Berlin and Kay surveyed a hundred languages in 1969 and found that color terms enter a language in a near-fixed order. A language at Stage I (the leftmost, almost no recorded human language sits here today) has only dark and light. Add red, and you have Stage II. Add either green or yellow for Stage III, both for Stage IV. Blue enters at Stage V — and that is roughly where Homer's Greek sat. Brown at VI, the remaining four (purple, pink, orange, grey) in any order at VII. Modern English, modern Korean, modern Japanese all sit at Stage VII; the Pirahã do not appear to have left Stage I.

whorfQuiz.title: Same colour, or different? — a Whorf reaction test
whorfQuiz.hint: Click Same or Different as fast as you can
whorfQuiz.stageAria: A simple speeded reaction test. Two coloured patches appear briefly side by side; the reader clicks Same or Different. Pairs near the linguistic boundary between blue and green (or between Russian siniy and goluboy) are reacted to faster than pairs of equal physical distance within a single name. The average reaction time over 20 trials is reported as a measure of where the reader's mental colour boundaries lie.
whorfQuiz.cap: Twelve trials of a paired-colour decision task. Each trial flashes two colour patches; press Same if you would give them the same name in your language, Different otherwise. Reaction times within a single named category (two blues you would both call blue) are typically slower than reactions across a category boundary (one you would call blue, one green), even when the physical distance between the patches is identical. Russian speakers, who have separate basic terms for dark and light blue (siniy, goluboy), are measurably faster at the boundary between those two than English speakers are anywhere inside English blue (Winawer et al., 2007). The effect is small but real, and it is the cleanest experimental evidence we have for a weak version of the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis.

note.label: What's next
note.body: We end the book proper here, on the word. The Chronology that follows is a map of the named people and dated events the previous eleven chapters rested on; the Coda is a working palette generator — the small machine the whole essay was a manual for. Open them in any order. The book is yours to fold.

chronology.title: A Chronology
chronology.standfirst: Three and a half centuries of color, on one line.
chronology.intro: The story has names and dates. Here they are — the figures and publications that this essay has leaned on, from Newton's first prism to the colour space that ships in browsers today.

fig.stageAria: A chronology of colour science and design, 1666 to 2023

events.title: Newton's prism, Woolsthorpe
events.blurb: During the plague years, at his family estate in Lincolnshire, Newton darkens a room and demonstrates that white light is a mixture, separable into the colors of the spectrum.

events.title: Newton, Opticks
events.blurb: The treatise that named the colors of light and founded the science of optics.

events.title: Goethe, Zur Farbenlehre
events.blurb: The artist's reply — colour as experience, attended to with phenomenological care.

events.title: Chevreul, De la loi du contraste simultané
events.blurb: Working at the Gobelins tapestry works, the chemist names the law that every colour is read against its neighbours.

events.title: Young–Helmholtz trichromatic theory
events.blurb: Hermann von Helmholtz formalises Thomas Young's earlier conjecture: human vision rests on three receptor types.

events.title: Bezold's pattern observations
events.blurb: Wilhelm von Bezold notices that fine stripes do not heighten contrast but blur into their field — the assimilation effect of Chapter Eight.

events.title: Munsell, the first measured colour solid
events.blurb: Albert Munsell gives each colour three plain coordinates — hue, value, chroma — and draws the solid as it is rather than as geometry wishes it.

events.title: Itten at the Bauhaus
events.blurb: Johannes Itten, teaching the Vorkurs in Weimar, codifies the twelve-hue colour wheel and the harmonies on it; his book, Kunst der Farbe, follows in 1961.

events.title: CIE 1931 chromaticity diagram
events.blurb: The Commission internationale de l'éclairage publishes the standard-observer table — the horseshoe of Chapter Seven.

events.title: Kubelka & Munk pigment theory
events.blurb: Paul Kubelka and Franz Munk publish the arithmetic of paint mixing — scattering and absorption together — and explain why ultramarine and cadmium yellow become green.

events.title: Albers, Interaction of Color
events.blurb: Josef Albers's slim volume teaches that colour is the most relative medium in art — its lesson made flesh in Chapter Eight.

events.title: CIE L*a*b*
events.blurb: The first widely used attempt at a perceptually uniform colour space — improved on, half a century later, by OKLab.

events.title: sRGB proposed
events.blurb: Hewlett-Packard and Microsoft propose the colour space that, formalised as IEC 61966-2-1 in 1999, becomes the default of the web and most consumer screens.

events.title: Display P3 on consumer screens
events.blurb: Apple ships a wider-gamut variant of DCI-P3 (2010) on its iMacs and, soon after, iPhones — expanding the screen colours of Chapter Seven beyond the older sRGB boundary.

events.title: Ottosson, OKLab
events.blurb: Björn Ottosson publishes a perceptually uniform colour space tuned to modern data — at last, equal steps look equal.

events.title: CSS Color 4 in major browsers
events.blurb: OKLCH, P3, and the new colour functions ship to almost every browser made — the essay's mathematics, now writable directly in a stylesheet.

coda.title: A Palette of Your Own
coda.standfirst: The essay is read. Here is what it was for.
coda.leadIn: Ten chapters on color are, in the end, in the service of one ordinary and joyful act: choosing colors that belong together. So here is a parting gift — a small machine that does just that, the way the essay taught it. Every palette it offers is raised on a real harmony from Chapter Six, its five colors spaced by the honest measure of Chapter Seven. Press the button; then press it again.

spectralDesc: The shortest waves the eye admits. Sensitivity is low here — the violet looks dim however bright the light.
Short waves. The S cone is near its peak; the world of sky and shadow.
The blue-green hinge, where the S and M cones trade the lead.
Medium waves. The eye is most alert here — green reads as the brightest hue of all.
The L and M cones fire almost together. A small shift in wavelength swings the hue quickly.
Long waves. The L cone dominates; the M cone is fading out.
The longest waves the eye can catch. Past this edge lies infrared — heat you feel but cannot see.

harmoniesCap.complementary: Two hues straight across the wheel — the sharpest contrast a pair can hold.
harmoniesCap.analogous: Three neighbouring hues — one family, quietly at ease together.
harmoniesCap.triadic: Three hues an equal third of the circle apart — balanced, lively, and stable.
harmoniesCap.split: A base hue with the two neighbours of its complement — tension, gently softened.
harmoniesCap.tetradic: Four hues at the wheel's quarter-points — two complementary pairs, a rich chord that wants one color to lead.
harmoniesCap.monochromatic: A single hue, varied only in value and chroma — the most serene scheme of all.
